reasons: Lake record is verified and identifies Maryland v. Buie as a U.S. Supreme Court case from 1990.

defect.evidence_quote: without probable cause or reasonable suspicion, look in closets and other spaces immediately adjoining the place of arrest
defect.problem: The holding field is truncated with an ellipsis and omits the limiting language needed to make the no-suspicion tier accurate, as well as the beyond-that reasonable-suspicion tier.
defect.proposed_fix: Complete the holding: no suspicion is needed only for closets and other spaces immediately adjoining the arrest location from which an attack could be launched; beyond that, a sweep requires articulable facts supporting a reasonable belief of danger and must remain cursory and limited.

reasons: The opinion supports a two-tier protective-sweep rule, but the asserted holding stops mid-phrase after "look in…".
As framed, the holding is under-specified and could be read too broadly without the immediate-adjoining limitation.
residual_risks: The body Rule section states the complete rule more accurately than the front matter holding.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Replace the truncated holding with the complete two-tier rule.

reasons: The opinion defines and applies protective sweeps as officer-safety searches incident to in-home arrest, which fits the Securing the Scene home.
The case supplies the governing Supreme Court rule for when officers may sweep adjoining spaces and other areas during an in-home arrest, supporting the Key — Anchor role.
residual_risks: The disclosed files do not include a separate taxonomy definition for Key — Anchor, so the role is verified from the opinion’s central rule and SCOTUS status.
